author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Rhode Island vineyards are intensifying surveillance for spotted lanternflies as the invasive insect becomes established across all five counties.

The Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management says the species was first detected in Warwick in 2021, with the state’s first confirmed population identified near Route 7 in Smithfield the following year. Growers told NBC 10 they are working with RIDEM and University of Rhode Island researchers who regularly check monitoring traps.

Spotted lanternflies feed on sap from grapevines and other plants. Large infestations can weaken vines, reduce yields and leave plants more vulnerable to cold. Their sugary waste can also encourage sooty mold. Tree-of-heaven is a preferred host, so its presence near vineyards is one factor growers watch.

Researchers are studying possible controls, including a parasitoid that attacks lanternfly nymphs, but no biological-control agent is currently approved for release in Rhode Island. For now, early detection, reporting and removal of egg masses remain central tools. Residents should use RIDEM guidance before handling suspected insects or moving outdoor materials that may carry eggs.
dek: The invasive insect is established in all five counties, prompting vineyards and state researchers to expand monitoring of vines and nearby host trees.
headline: Spotted lanternfly spread puts Rhode Island vineyards on watch
